application_questions.question: A Year 9 cohort has $40$ students in Class A (mean $71$) and $60$ students in Class B. If the overall cohort mean is $77$, find the mean score of Class B.
Nine daily temperatures have $\text{Mean} = 22^\circ\text{C}$. When a $10\text{th}$ day is added, the mean rises to $23.5^\circ\text{C}$. What was the temperature on the $10\text{th}$ day?
A media article claims 'Average salary in our town jumped $15\%$ this year', based on the arithmetic mean. Explain how this could happen even if $90\%$ of residents received no pay rise.
application_questions.answer: If a handful of ultra-high earners moved into the town or received massive bonuses, the mean would jump $15\%$ while the median salary remained completely unchanged.

application_questions.question: Two datasets have identical five-number summaries ($10, 20, 30, 40, 50$), yet Dataset A has values clustered tightly around $20$ and $40$ (bimodal) while Dataset B is clustered around $30$ (unimodal). What does this show about five-number summaries?
application_questions.answer: A five-number summary captures centre and spread at the quartiles, but cannot distinguish bimodal from unimodal shapes inside the quartiles; a stem plot or histogram is still needed.

reasoning_questions.question: Prove algebraically that if $y_i = ax_i + b$ with $a > 0$, then $\text{IQR}_y = a \cdot \text{IQR}_x$.
reasoning_questions.answer: Since $a > 0$ preserves order, $Q_{1,y} = a Q_{1,x} + b$ and $Q_{3,y} = a Q_{3,x} + b$. Subtracting gives $\text{IQR}_y = (a Q_{3,x} + b) - (a Q_{1,x} + b) = a(Q_{3,x} - Q_{1,x}) = a \cdot \text{IQR}_x$.

reasoning_questions.question: Under what condition is it possible for a dataset's lower outlier fence $Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ to be negative even when all data values are positive?
reasoning_questions.answer: Whenever $1.5 \times \text{IQR} > Q_1$ (i.e., $\text{IQR} > \frac{2}{3}Q_1$), which commonly happens in right-skewed positive data where $Q_1$ is small relative to $Q_3$.

application_questions.question: A non-linear scatterplot of braking distance $d$ (m) vs car speed $v$ (km/h) follows $d = 0.008v^2$. Find $d$ at $v = 50\text{ km/h}$ and $v = 100\text{ km/h}$, and explain why a linear model would underestimate braking distance at high speeds.
application_questions.answer: At $50\text{ km/h}$: $20\text{ m}$; at $100\text{ km/h}$: $80\text{ m}$ ($4\times$ as far when speed doubles). A linear model grows only $2\times$ and dangerously underestimates high-speed stopping distance.

application_questions.question: In a clinical trial, $40\%$ of Group A (receiving a new drug) improved vs $38\%$ of Group B (placebo). Why is it essential to know the sample sizes before concluding the drug works, and what role does random assignment play?
application_questions.answer: Small sample sizes (e.g. $n = 10$) mean a $2\%$ difference could be pure random chance; random assignment balances lurking variables between the two groups.

application_questions.question: A two-way table compares University Degree (Yes/No) with Income $> \$100\text{k}$ (Yes/No). Among $200$ graduates, $90$ earn $> \$100\text{k}$; among $300$ non-graduates, $60$ earn $> \$100\text{k}$. Calculate both conditional percentages and test for association.
A line of best fit has equation $y = -0.8x + 64$ with mean point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y}) = (30, 40)$. If a new point $(30, 40)$ is added to the dataset, does the mean point change? Explain.
application_questions.answer: No; adding a point equal to the existing mean $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ leaves both $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$ unchanged.

reasoning_questions.question: Why does a well-fitted line of best fit always have a sum of residuals $\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i) \approx 0$ when it passes through the mean point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$?
reasoning_questions.answer: If $\hat{y}_i = m x_i + c$ passes through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$, then $c = \bar{y} - m\bar{x}$, so $\sum (y_i - m x_i - c) = \sum y_i - m\sum x_i - n(\bar{y} - m\bar{x}) = n\bar{y} - m n\bar{x} - n\bar{y} + m n\bar{x} = 0$.

reasoning_questions.question: Explain the difference between an observational bivariate study and a randomised controlled experiment when investigating whether screen time causes poor sleep.
reasoning_questions.answer: An observational study only measures existing habits and cannot rule out lurking variables (like stress or caffeine), whereas a randomised experiment actively assigns participants to screen-time limits to isolate cause and effect.
